tier_reason: The page table has every number in the claim: aquatic_udp io_uring vs its own mio (epoll) backend vs opentracker, 1-16 cores, on a Hetzner CCX63 (AMD EPYC 7003 Milan) with rustc 1.76.0 and GCC 12.2.0 stated. The code is public: crates/bencher (the UDP runners are in crates/bencher/src/protocols/udp.rs). At the pinned commit 21a5301, scripts/bench/setup-udp-bookworm.sh fixes the flags: cargo profile release-debug (opt-level=3, thin LTO) with -C target-cpu=native minus AVX-512, and opentracker at -O3 -march=native -mtune=native. This is borderline A because the CPU is named only as the EPYC 7003 series on that instance type, with no SKU.

corrections.baseline: epoll (aquatic_udp's own mio backend, which uses epoll on Linux); also opentracker (C), which the bencher runs with 'listen.udp.workers N', so it uses N pthreads doing blocking recvfrom on one shared socket rather than its libowfat epoll event loop
corrections.claimed_speedup: Average responses/s, best result. At 16 cores: aquatic_udp (io_uring) 2,258,321 vs aquatic_udp (mio/epoll) 2,037,713 (~1.11x) and opentracker 1,645,828 (~1.37x). At 1 core: io_uring 226,065 vs mio 186,939 (~1.21x) and opentracker 190,540 (~1.19x). Ratios derived from page data. The win is not uniform: at 12 cores io_uring (1,837,223) is slightly below mio (1,871,353).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.76.0, GCC 12.2.0 and go 1.19.8 (stated on page). Flags come from scripts/bench/setup-udp-bookworm.sh at the pinned aquatic commit 21a5301: aquatic is built with cargo --profile release-debug (inherits release: opt-level=3, lto="thin", plus debug info) and RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' with AVX-512 target features disabled (scripts/env-native-cpu-without-avx-512); opentracker's Makefile is edited to OPTS_production=-O3 -march=native -mtune=native; chihaya uses a plain go build.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 622 stars; the aquatic and aquatic_udp READMEs list the explodie.org public tracker (udp://explodie.org:6969, typically serving ~100,000 req/s) and webtorrent.dev as known users of aquatic
corrections.caveats: The benchmark was written and run by the aquatic maintainer, although opentracker and chihaya are third-party implementations. The io_uring backend is an experimental opt-in cargo feature ('io-uring', Linux 6.0+); the default build uses mio/epoll. The io_uring advantage over mio is small (~1.1-1.2x) and reverses at 12 cores. In this setup opentracker uses blocking-recvfrom worker threads, not epoll. The CPU is given only as AMD EPYC 7003 (Milan) on a Hetzner CCX63, with no exact SKU. Chihaya (Go) trails by ~10x and crashes under high load, per the bencher README. The results date from 2024-02-10 (commit 21a5301).

notes: The numbers match the page exactly. I corrected three things. The 'opentracker is epoll-based' framing is wrong for this setup: ot_udp.c's udp_worker threads loop on a blocking socket_recv6, and the bencher sets listen.udp.workers. The explodie.org ~100k req/s tracker is an aquatic user, not an opentracker figure. The flags are itemized in the pinned setup script. The metadata checks out (Apache-2.0, 622 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-07-13, active).

tier_reason: benchmarks/benchmarks.md (io-uring-feat-fast-poll branch, Feb 2020) has req/s tables for the io_uring server and the author's epoll server (frevib/epoll-echo-server) at 1-1000 clients and 128/512/1000-byte messages. The claimed peaks (216,637 vs 152,561) and 1000-client figures (173,343 vs 108,380) are there. The code and flags are public (both Makefiles use -Wall -O2 -D_GNU_SOURCE; the client is rust_echo_bench, and a run script is on the page), but there is no compiler version or CPU model (only 'Macbook pro 6-core 2,6 GHz' under a VMware VM), so this is first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 128-byte messages, req/s: io_uring peaks at 216,637 (300 clients) vs epoll's peak of 152,561 (150 clients), ~1.4x; at 1000 clients, io_uring 173,343 vs epoll 108,380, ~1.6x (ratios derived from page data). With 1 client the two are equal (13,093 vs 13,177). The 512- and 1000-byte tables show similar margins.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Both servers are built with -Wall -O2 -D_GNU_SOURCE: the io_uring Makefile on branch io-uring-feat-fast-poll has CCFLAGS ?= -Wall -O2 -D_GNU_SOURCE -luring against the bundled liburing, and the frevib/epoll-echo-server Makefile runs gcc -Wall -O2 -D_GNU_SOURCE. The compiler version is not stated. The client (rust_echo_bench) is run with cargo run --release.
corrections.hardware: MacBook Pro host: 6 cores, 2.6 GHz, 32 GB RAM (CPU model not named). Guest: VMware Ubuntu 18.04 with 8 GB RAM and 6 vcores (3 physical cores), Linux 5.6.0-rc1+ with IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL (io_uring-task-poll branch). 2 vcores (one physical core) isolated with isolcpus=0,1, with the echo server pinned to CPU 0 via taskset.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 400 stars; linked in at least 7 Hacker News comments across io_uring threads from 2020 to 2025 (HN Algolia API); the Twitter references could not be checked
corrections.caveats: Both servers were written by the same author to isolate epoll vs io_uring. The CPU model and compiler version are not stated, and the run was in a VMware VM on a laptop. The benchmark dates from 2020-02-29 on a pre-mainline IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL kernel (5.6.0-rc1+), so it may not reflect current io_uring. It covers the io-uring-feat-fast-poll branch; master moved to IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS (Linux 5.7+) and the README labels the page 'without buffer selection'. The page reports that the io_uring server became unresponsive (uninterruptible sleep) under sustained load and had to be restarted between message sizes, while the epoll server had no such problem. Both servers crash above ~2000 clients.

notes: The numbers match the page exactly. The tier stays C: the code and -O2 flags are public, but there is no compiler version and no CPU model. The fixes are the '(derived from page data)' marking, the server flags (the record said they were unstated; both Makefiles have -O2), and the hardware detail. The metadata checks out (MIT, 400 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2024-01-20, stale). The epoll baseline repo is also MIT (53 stars, last pushed 2020-02-29).

tier_reason: The README Benchmark section has pingpong echo-server output (4 threads, 1000 connections, 10s) with libevent 157, libev 210, libuv 156, libhv 215, asio 132 and poco 165 MB/s, matching the claim. The harness is public (echo-servers/build.sh, benchmark.sh, pingpong_client.cpp and the per-library *_echo.c/cpp; Makefile target echo-servers builds them with -O3). The README run (added 2021-03-09) states no compiler, library versions or CPU, so it is first-party C. Current GitHub Actions runs (ubuntu-24.04, gcc 13.3.0, runner CPU not logged) use a different config (2 threads, 100 connections) but show the same ordering against libevent and libuv.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README pingpong run (4 threads, 1000 connections, 10s, 1024-byte messages): libhv 215 MB/s vs libevent 157 MB/s (~1.37x) and libuv 156 MB/s (~1.38x); it also beats poco (165) and asio (132) and trails libev (210). Ratios derived from page data. Three GitHub Actions runs on 2026-09-25 (benchmark.yml, 2 threads, 100 connections) are consistent: libhv 115/207/120 MB/s vs libevent 79/149/81 (~1.39-1.48x) and libuv 77/125/73 (~1.49-1.66x). In those runs libhv is at parity with libev (118/212/119) and asio (118/211/115), so the README's win over asio is not reproduced.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile target echo-servers compiles each echo server and pingpong_client with -g -Wall -O3 (-std=c99 or c++11). libhv itself is built with the default BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE (-O2, -DNDEBUG). libevent, libev, libuv, asio and poco are distro packages (apt/yum/brew via echo-servers/build.sh). No compiler or library versions are given for the README run. The current CI run uses gcc 13.3.0 on ubuntu-24.04 with libevent 2.1.12, libev 4.33 and libuv 1.48.0.
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the README run. The current CI runs use GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest (ubuntu-24.04) runners; the CPU model is not logged.
corrections.workload: pingpong echo-servers benchmark (echo-servers/benchmark.sh + pingpong_client): a single-event-loop TCP echo server per library, loaded over loopback by the libhv-based pingpong_client with 4 threads, 1000 connections, 1024-byte messages for 10s, measuring aggregate read throughput (MB/s). The CI version uses 2 threads and 100 connections.
corrections.caveats: All echo servers and the pingpong client were written by the libhv author, and the client is itself built on libhv. The baselines are simple implementations: the libuv server mallocs a buffer per read plus a write request per echo, and the libevent server allocates an evbuffer per read. The README numbers come from a 2021-03-09 run whose 4-thread/1000-connection setting was pingpong_client's default at the time; they cannot be traced to a CI run, and today's CI uses 2 threads and 100 connections. Compiler and library versions and the CPU are not stated for the README run. CI numbers swing ~1.8x between runners, though the ordering holds. The margin over libevent and libuv is modest (~1.4-1.6x), and libhv ties libev and (in current CI) asio.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly and the tier stays C. The record's claim that the README numbers came from GitHub Actions is not supported: the README run used 4 threads and 1000 connections, while benchmark.sh (and so CI) has defaulted to 2 threads and 100 connections since 2021-11. The three latest CI logs still show libhv ~1.4-1.7x over libevent and libuv but tied with libev and asio. The metadata checks out (BSD-3-Clause, 7,555 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-09-25, active).
